paragraphs.text:
Of Gregory, among the saints, on the text: "When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected."

All the words of the Lord are pure and clean words, as the Prophet says, whenever the mind, cleansed of every heretical assumption like silver refined in the fire, holds the words in their own proper radiance, the radiance that belongs to truth by nature. Above all, I think, we must bear witness that the teachings of the holy Paul have every brilliance and purity. He was initiated in paradise into the knowledge of things not to be spoken, and he had Christ speaking within him. So he said the kind of things we would expect from someone taught by such a teacher, with the Word as his guide and teacher. But the wicked [?] try to make the divine silver counterfeit, dimming the radiance of the Word by mixing in heretical and adulterated notions. Either they fail to understand the Apostle's mystical thoughts, or they maliciously take them in whatever sense suits them, and they drag them in to plead the cause of their own wickedness. They say that the apostolic text supports them in lowering the [?] of the only-begotten God, the text that says, "Then the Son will be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him," as though this phrase showed some servile lowliness. For this reason it seemed necessary to examine carefully what the passage means, so as to show that the apostolic silver is truly pure, separate from every filthy and heretical notion and unmixed with them. We know, then, from the usage of holy Scripture, that this word has many meanings and is not always fitted to the same ideas. At one time it means one thing, and at another it indicates something else. For example, "Slaves,"

it says, "must be subject to their own masters." And about irrational nature, which was subjected to man by God, the Prophet says, "You have subjected all things under his feet." And about those conquered in war he says, "He subjected peoples to us, and nations under our feet." Again, recalling those who are saved through knowledge, he speaks as if in the person of God: "Foreigners have been subjected to me." Closely related to this, it seems, is the verse we examined in the sixty-first psalm: "Will not my soul be subjected to God?" Besides all these there is the text our enemies bring against us from the Epistle to the Corinthians: "Then the Son himself will be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him." Since this word, then, carries many senses, it would be well to separate each of them and consider which meaning of subjection properly fits the Apostle's saying. We say, then, that with those conquered in war by the power of the victors, subjection means bowing to the conquerors unwillingly and under compulsion. For if the captives gain any strength that gives them hope of overcoming their masters, they rise up again against those who conquered them, judging it an outrage and a disgrace to be subject to their enemies. Irrational creatures are subject to rational ones in another way: by nature they lack the greatest of goods, that is, reason. So the inferior must be subject to the one that is better endowed by nature. Those held under the yoke of slavery by some legal process may be equal in nature. Yet because they cannot resist the law, they accept the rank of subjects, driven into subjection by an inescapable necessity. But the goal of our subjection to God is salvation, as we learned from the prophecy that says, "Be subject to God, my soul, for from him is my salvation." When our opponents, then, bring forward the Apostle's word saying that the Son will be subjected to the Father, it would be fitting to ask them, given the distinct meanings of this word, which meaning of subjection they have in view when they think the word must be applied to the only-begotten God. But clearly they will not say that they understand the Son's subjection in any of the senses mentioned. He was not an enemy brought into subjection through war, who might hope and strive to rise again against the one who rules him. Nor, as with irrational creatures, does the Word have a subjection that is necessary by nature through some lack of the good, as sheep, cattle and oxen have toward man. Nor is he like bought or home-born slaves, enslaved by law, who wait for goodwill or favor

to set them free some day from the yoke of slavery. [?] the incorruptible, the blessed, the one who is always the same, who can become neither better nor worse. He admits no addition in goodness and no inclination toward the worse. The one from whom salvation flows to others does not himself lack someone to save him. Which meaning of subjection, then, will they reasonably say properly applies to him? For all the senses we have examined proved to be far from anything that could properly be thought or said of the only-begotten God. We might also add the kind of subjection mentioned in the Gospel according to Luke: the Lord, when he had reached his twelfth year, "was subject to his parents." But neither would this fit being said of the one who is before the ages and true, in relation to his true Father. In that case, the one who was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin, also accepted to advance through the ages of our nature. As an infant he took an infant's food, eating butter and honey. In the same way, as he advanced to boyhood, he did not refuse what was suitable and fitting for that age, and so became a model of good order for life. In other people the understanding is imperfect in such matters, and youth needs guidance toward what is better from those more mature. For this reason the twelve-year-old is subject to his mother, to show that whatever is perfected through progress rightly accepts subjection as a guide to the good before it reaches perfection. But the one who is always perfect in every good can admit neither progress nor diminution in himself, because his nature lacks nothing and cannot be diminished. Why such a one would be subjected, those who say everything without thinking could not explain. When he lived among human nature in the flesh, he laid down subjection for the young by what he did in his childhood. This is clear from the fact that once he reached full maturity he no longer looked to his mother's authority. When she urged him at Cana of Galilee to show his power, since the wedding feast was running short, and to supply the banquet with the wine it needed, he did not refuse to grant the favor to those in need. But he declined his mother's counsel as no longer suited to his time of life, saying, "Woman, what have I to do with you?" Do you want to direct me even at this age? Has my hour not yet come, the hour that gives my age self-rule and independence?

If, then, during his life in the flesh the proper measure of maturity threw off subjection to the one who bore him, no one could say what place subjection has in the [?] of the one who is sovereign over the age in his own dominion. For it is proper to the divine and blessed life always to remain the same and never to admit change through alteration. The Word who was in the beginning, the only-begotten God, is a stranger to all deviation and alteration. How, then, can he become later what he is not now? For the Apostle does not speak as though the Son were always subjected, but as one who will be subjected at the end, when the whole universe is brought to completion. Yet if subjection is a good thing and worthy to be said of God, how is this good now absent from God? It must surely be equally good for both: for the Son who is subjected and for the Father who receives the Son's subjection. Then at present such a good would be lacking to both the Father and the Son. What neither the Father nor the Son had before the ages would be added to the Father and the Son when time is completed. The one would undergo subjection, and the other would thereby receive some addition and increase of his own glory, which for the present he does not have. Where, then, is unchangeableness in this? For to become something later that one is not now is proper to a nature that can change. So either subjection is good, and we ought to believe that this good belongs to God now as well, or such a thing is unworthy of God, and then it belongs to him neither now nor at any other time. But the Apostle says that the Son will be subjected then, not that he is subjected now. So the saying looks to some other purpose, and the meaning of the word is far from the malice of the heretics. What, then, is the meaning? Perhaps one could better grasp the sense from the context of what is written in this passage. Paul had taken up a polemical argument against the Corinthians. They had accepted faith in the Lord, but they thought the doctrine of human resurrection was a myth, saying, "How are the dead raised? And with what kind of body do they come?" After death their bodies had vanished in many and various ways, either through decay or consumed by flesh-eating creatures: reptiles, fish, birds and four-footed beasts. For this reason he set many arguments before them. He urged them not to make God's power equal to their own, and not to think that whatever is impossible for man is impossible for God as well. Instead, they should judge the greatness of divine authority from examples familiar to us. So he sets before them the marvel of the bodies of seeds, which are constantly renewed by divine power. He shows how the wisdom of God was not at a loss to devise countless kinds of bodies throughout the universe: rational and irrational, creatures of the air and of the land, and those displayed to us in the heavens, the sun and the other stars. Each of these came into being by divine power, and so gives us [?] that God would not be at a loss for our bodies at the resurrection either

a demonstration. For all existing things were not refashioned out of some underlying matter into their visible form. Rather, the divine will itself became the matter and substance of the things created. If so, it is far more possible to restore what already exists to its own form than for what did not exist at the beginning to come into subsistence and being. In his words to them Paul showed that the first man was dissolved into earth through sin, and was therefore called "earthy." So it followed that all who came from him, born of such a man, became earthy and mortal like him. He then necessarily added the second sequence, by which man is formed anew from mortality to immortality. In the same way, he says, the good came into our nature and was poured out from one to all, just as evil was poured out through one to the multitude by the succession of those born after him. He uses these words to establish his teaching on this: "The first man," he says, "was from the earth, earthy; the second is from heaven. As was the earthy one, so are those who are earthy; and as is the heavenly one, so are those who are heavenly. And just as we have borne the image of the earthy one, so let us also bear the image of the heavenly one." With these and similar reasonings he strengthened the argument for the resurrection. Through many other arguments he entangled the heretics in syllogisms, showing that anyone who disbelieves the resurrection of human beings does not accept the resurrection of Christ either. By a chain of connected propositions he drew an inescapable conclusion, saying, "If there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ has not been raised either. And if Christ has not been raised, faith in him is also in vain." The premise is true, that Christ has been raised from the dead. So what is connected to it must also be true, that there is a resurrection of the dead. For when the particular case is proved, the universal is proved along with it. And conversely, if someone says the universal claim is false, that there is a resurrection of the dead, then the particular claim will not be found true either, that Christ has been raised from the dead. For what is universally impossible will not be possible in any single case. But for those who have received the Word it is certain and beyond dispute that Christ has been raised from the dead. So in the particular faith in Christ's resurrection, the universal will also necessarily be believed. In this way he forced them by syllogism to accept the doctrine, by saying, "If there is not..." (for what does not exist universally cannot exist in any single case, but if we believe that he has been raised, faith about him becomes proof of the universal resurrection of human beings). He then added to the argument the saying that brings the whole proof of this doctrine to its conclusion: "For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive." Here he clearly unveils the mystery concerning this, which he has in view in what follows, and by a necessary sequence he directs the argument toward the goal of our hopes.

The aim of what happens is this. I will first set out in my own words the sense of what is written, and then add the Apostle's words, which fit the sense I have set out. What, then, is the aim of the teaching the divine Apostle lays down in that passage? It is that at some time the nature of evil will pass away into non-being, vanishing completely from existence. The divine and pure goodness will contain every rational nature within itself, and none of the things made by God will fall away from the kingdom of God. All the evil mixed into existing things will be dissolved, like some adulterated material, by the smelting of the purifying fire. Then everything that had its origin from God will become as it was at the beginning, when it had not yet received evil. And he says that this happens as follows. The pure and undefiled divinity of the Only-begotten came to be in the mortal and perishable nature of human beings. From the whole of human nature, with which the divine was mingled, the man in Christ was formed as a kind of firstfruits of the common lump, and through him all humanity was joined to the divinity. In him the whole nature of evil was abolished, for he "committed no sin," as the prophet says, "nor was deceit found in his mouth." Along with sin, the death that follows it was also abolished in him, for death has no other origin than sin. So the abolition of evil and the destruction of death began from him. Then a kind of order was imposed on what happens, following a certain sequence. Whatever is found farther from the first or closer to him, as the good descends by degrees, follows the one who leads according to the rank and power that each has. First comes the man in Christ. He became the firstfruits of our nature by receiving the divinity into himself. He also became the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep and the firstborn from the dead, having loosed the pangs of death. This man was wholly separate from sin, and in himself he abolished the might of death and destroyed all its rule and authority and power. After him, if someone like Paul is found, who became as far as possible an imitator of Christ in turning away from evil, such a person will follow behind the firstfruits at the time of his coming. And again (I say this by way of hypothesis) perhaps Timothy will follow, who imitated his teacher in himself as far as he could, or someone else like him. And so on in order, with all those who, by falling a little short in goodness, are found behind those who always go ahead. This continues until the line of followers reaches those in whom evil abounds and the share of the better is found to be smaller. In the same proportion, the sequence arranges those who return to the better, from those who have less of evil to those who exceed in evil,

until the advance of the good reaches the utmost limit of evil and wipes out wickedness. This is indeed the goal of our hope: that nothing opposed to the good will be left, but that the divine life, passing through all things, will wipe death out of existence entirely. Sin, from which, as has been said, death gained its reign over human beings, will have been removed first. When, then, every evil authority and rule in us has been destroyed, and no passion any longer dominates our nature, then, with nothing else holding sway, all things must be subjected to the one who rules over all. And subjection to God is complete estrangement from evil. When, therefore, we all come to be outside evil in imitation of the firstfruits, then the whole [?] of our nature, mingled with the firstfruits and become one continuous body, will accept the rule of the good alone over itself. And so, when the whole body of our nature has been blended with the divine and pure nature, the subjection that is called the Son's comes about through us. The subjection accomplished in his body is referred to him, who worked the grace of subjection in us. This, then, as far as we have understood it, is the sense of what the great Paul taught. And it would be a good time to set out the Apostle's own words, which run as follows: "For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive. But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then those who belong to Christ at his coming. Then comes the end, when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father, when he has abolished every rule and authority and power. For he must reign until he has put his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be abolished is death. For he has subjected all things under his feet. But when it says that all things have been subjected, it is clear that this does not include the one who subjected all things to him. And when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all." In the last of these words he clearly presents the nonexistence of evil, when he says that God comes to be in all things and becomes all things to each one. For clearly it will be true that God is in all things only when no evil is found in existing things. It is not fitting for God to be in evil. So either he will not be in all things, if some evil is left among existing things, or, if we must truly believe that he is in all things, then the nonexistence of evil is shown along with our faith in this. For God cannot come to be in evil. And God's becoming all things to existing beings shows the simplicity and oneness of the life we hope for. By this phrase Paul shows that our life will no longer be pieced together from many different things, as the present life is. Instead, God becomes for us all the things that seem necessary for this life, each of them being taken up, by a kind of analogy, into something more divine. So both food

…that God is for us, in a manner befitting God, food to be eaten [?], and drink, and likewise clothing and shelter, air, place, wealth, enjoyment, beauty, health, strength, wisdom, glory, blessedness, and everything counted as part of the good lot that our nature needs, when the meaning of these words is raised to what befits God. From this we learn that whoever has come to be in God has everything in having him. To have God is nothing other than to be united to God. And no one could be united to him except by becoming one body with him, as Paul calls it. For all of us, joined to the one body of Christ by sharing in it, become his one body. So when the good has passed through all, then his whole body will be subjected to the life-giving power, and in this way the subjection of this body is said to be the subjection of the Son himself, who is blended with his own body, which is the Church. So the Apostle says to the Colossians, in these words: "Now I rejoice in my sufferings, and in my flesh I fill up what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ, for the sake of his body, which is the Church, of which I became a minister according to the dispensation." And to the Church of the Corinthians he says: "You are the body of Christ, and members each in part." To the Ephesians he sets out the teaching on this more clearly, where he says: "Speaking the truth in love, let us grow up in every way into him who is the head, Christ, from whom the whole body, joined and knit together by every joint of its supply, according to the working in the measure of each single part, makes the body grow so that it builds itself up in love." This means that Christ builds himself up through those who are continually added to the faith. He will stop building himself up when the growth and completion of his body reaches its proper measure, and nothing is any longer missing from the body that must be added by building, since all have been built upon the foundation of the prophets and apostles and have been added to the faith; when, as the Apostle says, "we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ." If, then, he who is the head builds up his body in order, through those who are continually added, joining and knitting all together into what each is by nature fitted for according to the measure of his working, so that one becomes a hand, another a foot, an eye, an ear, or some other of the parts that make up the body, according to the proportion of each one's faith, and in doing this he builds himself up, as has been said, then it is clear from this that, coming to be in all, he receives into himself all who are united to him through the communion of the body, and makes them all members of his own body, so that there are many members but one body. He, then, who united us to himself and was united to us, and having become one with

[?] us in all things, makes all that is ours his own. And the chief of our goods is subjection to the divine, when the whole creation comes to be of one voice with itself, and every knee bows to him, of things in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confesses that Jesus Christ is Lord. Then, when the whole creation has become one body, and all have grown together with one another in him through obedience, he refers to himself the subjection of his own body to the Father. Let no one be surprised at what is said. For we too, by a certain habit of speech, attribute to the soul what is done through our body. So that man, speaking to his own soul about the rich yield of his land, says, "Eat, drink, and be merry," and thereby refers the filling of the flesh to the soul. In the same way here the subjection of the body of the Church is referred to him who dwells in that body. And since everything that comes to be in him is saved, and salvation is interpreted as subjection, as the Psalm leads us to understand, it follows that in this passage of the Apostle we learn to believe that nothing remains outside those who are saved. The text signifies this by the destruction of death and by the subjection of the Son, because these two go together: that death should no longer exist at all, and that all should come to be in life. And the Lord is life, through whom, according to the Apostle's word, his whole body is brought to the Father, when he hands over our kingdom to God the Father. His body, as has often been said, is the whole of human nature, with which he was mingled. It is for this very reason that Paul called the Lord "mediator between God and men." For he who is in the Father and came to be among men fulfils his mediation in this: that he unites all to himself, and through himself to the Father. So the Lord says in the Gospel, addressing the Father: "As you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us." This plainly shows that he who is in the Father, having united us to himself, brings about through himself our union with the Father. And what follows in the Gospel agrees with what has been said: "The glory which you have given me I have given them." By "glory" here I think he means the Holy Spirit, whom he gave to the disciples by breathing on them. For those who stand apart from one another cannot be united in any other way than by growing together in the unity of the Spirit. "For if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him." And the Spirit is the glory, as he says elsewhere to the Father: "Glorify me with the glory which I had with you from the beginning, before the world was." For God the Word, who before the world had the glory of the Father, became flesh in the last days; and the flesh too had to become, through its blending with the Word, that which the Word is. And it becomes so by receiving that which the Word had before the world. This was the Holy Spirit; for nothing else exists before the ages except the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. That is

why he says here too: "The glory which you have given me I have given them," so that through it they may be united to me, and through me to you. Let us look also at what is added next in the Gospel: "That they may be one, as we are one: you in me, and I in them, because I and you are one, so that they may be perfected into one." I do not think these words need any further explanation to be fitted to the meaning before us, since the words themselves plainly set out the teaching about these things. "That they may be one, as we are one." For it is not possible for all to become one, as we are one, in any other way than this: that, separated from everything that divides them from one another, they should be united to us who are one, "that they may be one, as we are one." And how does this come about? "Because I am in them." For it is not possible for me alone to come to be in them; you must certainly be there too, since I and you are one. And so those perfected in us will be perfected into one, for we are the one. He signifies this grace still more clearly in the words that follow, saying: "You have loved them as you have loved me." For if the Father loves the Son, and all of us who become his body through faith in him come to be in the Son, it follows that he who loves his own Son also loves the Son's body as he loves the Son himself. And we are the body. So by what has been said the Apostle's meaning has become clear: the subjection of the Son to the Father signifies the knowledge of him who is, and the salvation, that comes about for the whole of human nature. The argument could be made clearer for us from other thoughts of the Apostle as well. I will mention only one of them, out of caution declining the many testimonies so as not to stretch the discourse to great length. Paul says somewhere in his writings: "I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me." If, then, Paul, crucified with Christ, no longer lives, but Christ lives in him, everything Paul does and says is rightly referred to Christ who lives in him. Indeed he says that Paul's words are spoken by Christ, when he says: "Or do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?" And he says that his achievements for the Gospel are not his own, but ascribes them to the grace of Christ dwelling in him. If, then, Christ who lives in him is, as follows, said to work and speak what is his, and Paul, having turned away from everything that formerly ruled him, when he was a blasphemer, a persecutor and insolent, looks to the true good alone and makes himself obedient and submissive to it, then the subjection of Paul to God is also referred to him who lives in him, who both speaks the good things in Paul and does them. And the chief of all goods is subjection to God. What the argument has found in the case of one man may reasonably be applied to the whole human creation as well, when, as the Lord says, [?]

the Gospel has reached the whole world. For when all have put off the old man with his deeds and desires, and have received the Lord into themselves, then necessarily he who lives in them works the good things they do. And the highest of all goods is salvation, which comes to us by our being estranged from evil. But it is not possible to be separated from evil in any other way than by being blended with God through subjection. So this subjection to God is also referred to him who lives in us. "For if anything is beautiful, it is his; and if anything is good, it is from him," says one of the prophets. Since, then, subjection is beautiful and good, it has been shown to be his, and its goodness comes wholly from him from whom is the nature of every good, as the prophet's word says. But let no one, in view of the common usage [?]
